lessons.title: Integers, rational numbers and place value
lessons.summary: Sort numbers and convert between the figures and words for large whole numbers.
lessons.objective: Sort numbers and convert between the figures and words for large whole numbers.
lessons.before: Read one worked example. Cover the next step, try it, then compare your method.
lessons.ideas:
Start counting natural numbers at 1. Integers include zero and the negative whole numbers.

Calculate a square root when you can. The root of a perfect square is rational.

One million contains 1000 whole thousands. Include those when finding the total number of thousands.

Read each non-zero group and add its place name. In words, skip a zero group. In figures, keep all three digits for every group after the first.
lessons.method:
Which numbers are integers?

Integers occupy the whole-number marks on a number line. Fractions can sit between the marks.

Can I write the number as a fraction?

A rational number is a fraction of two integers with a non-zero denominator. A terminating decimal or a decimal with a repeating pattern is rational.

What does each group of digits count?

Read from the right in groups of three. The groups count ones, thousands, millions and billions. A zero keeps the digits in their correct columns.

How do I write a large number in words?

Start by splitting the digits into groups of three from the right. Label those groups ones, thousands, millions and billions.
mistakes: A number can have more than one label. For example, 5 is both natural and an integer.
An irrational number can have a rounded calculator display. The rounded decimal is a different number.
The middle group on its own does not give the total number of whole thousands.
A group of three zeros still holds a place. Without it, a billion can become a million.

examples.title: Find all the integers
examples.question: Find all the integers in this list: \(-5,\quad 0,\quad \frac{16}{3},\quad 7\).
examples.solution:
The whole-number ticks include \(-5\), \(0\) and \(7\).

\(\frac{16}{3}\) lies just above 5; there is a fractional part of \(\frac{1}{3}\).

Use all three integers: \(\{-5,0,7\}\).

examples.title: Spot an irrational number
examples.question:
Choose the irrational number.

A. \(\sqrt{16}\)   B. \(0.18\)   C. \(\sqrt{18}\)
examples.solution:
\(\sqrt{16}\) equals the integer 4. It is rational.

\(0.18\) ends, so it can be written as an exact fraction over 100.

18 lies strictly between consecutive perfect squares. Its square root \(\sqrt{18}\) is irrational.

examples.title: Read the thousands
examples.question: How many whole thousands are in \(4\,127\,043\)?
examples.solution:
The first group contributes 4 million, or 4000 thousand.

The middle group adds 127 thousand. The final 43 ones do not make another thousand.

The total is \(4000+127=4127\) whole thousands.

examples.title: Write a number in words
examples.question: Write \(5\,034\,000\,014\) in words.
examples.solution:
Split the digits from the right into groups of three.

Read the non-zero groups in order. The entries are 5 in the billions group, 34 in the millions group, 14 in the ones group.

Write five billion, thirty-four million and fourteen.

lessons.title: Factors, multiples and prime numbers
lessons.summary: Use factor pairs and multiplication lists to decide what kind of whole number you have.
lessons.objective: Use factor pairs and multiplication lists to decide what kind of whole number you have.
lessons.before: Read one worked example. Cover the next step, try it, then compare your method.
lessons.ideas:
Start at 1 and work upwards. Stop just before your next pair would reverse an earlier pair.

Look at the neighbouring multiples to show which one falls in the interval.

The number 2 is the only even prime. Odd numbers can be composite.
lessons.method:
How do I find every factor?

Arrange objects in equal rows with none left over. A possible row count and its column count give a factor pair.

How can I find a multiple inside a range?

A multiple is made by multiplying. Step along a times table and choose the values inside the bounds given in the question.

How can I tell whether a number is prime?

A prime is a positive integer with exactly two positive factors. A composite has an extra factor pair. If a larger factor exists beyond the square root, it has a smaller partner you have already tested.
mistakes: If both members of a pair are equal, list that factor once.
Greater than and less than both exclude equality. Check the endpoints.
The number 1 has one positive factor. It is neither prime nor composite.

examples.title: List every positive factor
examples.question: List all the positive factors of 12.
examples.solution:
Start with \(1\times12\). Try the next possible small divisors in order.

The full list of pairs is \(1\times12\), \(2\times6\), \(3\times4\). Stop when the next pair would reverse one you already have.

Collect both numbers from each pair: \(1,2,3,4,6,12\).

examples.title: Find a multiple inside a range
examples.question: Find the multiple of 8 that is greater than 30 and less than 35.
examples.solution:
The multiples of 8 are its times-table values.

The value \(8\times3=24\) is too small.

The next value is \(8\times4=32\) and it lies inside the range. The following value is too large.

examples.title: Identify a prime
examples.question:
Which number is prime?

A. \(27\)   B. \(29\)   C. \(1\)
examples.solution:
27 is composite because \(27=3\times9\).

One has only one positive factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.

No prime up to 5 divides 29, so 29 has exactly two positive factors.

lessons.title: Prime factor trees and prime powers
lessons.summary: Find the prime building blocks of a number and record them with powers.
lessons.objective: Find the prime building blocks of a number and record them with powers.
lessons.before: Read one worked example. Cover the next step, try it, then compare your method.
lessons.ideas:
Different first branches give the same prime factors when the tree is finished.

Count each prime separately. The exponent of 2 records only copies of 2.

Check whether each exponent is odd or even. Multiply the primes that need a partner.
lessons.method:
What belongs at the tips of a factor tree?

Split a number into two factors greater than 1. Split any composite factor again. Mark the prime tips and read those tips together.

Why do the exponents add?

An exponent counts repeated factors. When you multiply two products, the prime copies from both go into the same list.

How can I make the product a square?

A square uses the same factor list twice. So every prime copy must have a matching partner. Add one copy wherever the exponent is odd.
mistakes: A branch ending in 4 or 9 is unfinished. Every final factor must be prime.
Do not multiply the exponents when forming a product of powers with the same base.
A prime with no printed exponent has exponent 1.

examples.title: Use prime factorisation
examples.question: Use prime factorisation to find the exponent on 2 in 84.
examples.solution:
Split off 2 while the remaining number is even.

The prime factors in order are \(2\times 2\times 3\times 7\).

The compact form is \(84=2^{2}\times 3\times 7\). The exponent on 2 is 2.

examples.title: Combine repeated prime factors
examples.question: \(A=2^{3}\times 5,\quad B=2^{2}\times 7\). What is the exponent of 2 in the prime factorisation of \(AB\)?
examples.solution:
The factor list for A has 3 copies of 2. The list for B has 2.

Putting the lists together makes \(3+2=5\) copies of 2.

The result is \(AB=2^{5}\times 5\times 7\).

examples.title: Complete pairs to make a square
examples.question: Let \(N=2^{4}\times 3^{3}\times 5^{3}\times 7^{2}\). Find the smallest positive integer that makes a square when multiplied by \(N\).
examples.solution:
A square repeats the same list of factors twice. Every prime exponent must be even.

These primes have odd exponents: 3, 5. Each needs one more copy.

Multiply the needed primes. The smallest multiplier is 15.

lessons.title: Highest common factor and lowest common multiple
lessons.summary: Choose the right operation for equal groups and repeating cycles.
lessons.objective: Choose the right operation for equal groups and repeating cycles.
lessons.before: Read one worked example. Cover the next step, try it, then compare your method.
lessons.ideas:
For the HCF keep only the prime copies found in both factor lists.

The common start at zero has already happened. Find the next shared time.

HCF: take the smaller power of every shared prime. LCM: take the larger power of every prime used.
lessons.method:
What is the largest number of identical groups?

The number of groups divides each of the supplies. The highest common factor gives the greatest possible number of identical groups.

When do the two events next meet?

Start both timelines at zero. Mark the times of each repeating event on its own line. The first positive time marked on both lines is the lowest common multiple.

How do I choose between HCF and LCM?

Ask which way the division goes. A group count divides both totals. A shared elapsed time can be divided by both periods.
mistakes: Read whether the question wants the number of groups or the number in each group.
The product of the periods is a common multiple. A smaller common multiple may come first.
Convert to the same units before comparing times. Keep the answer in the units requested.

examples.title: Make the most identical packs
examples.question: A workshop has 27 brass clips and 45 steel clips. It makes identical packs and uses every clip. What is the greatest possible number of packs?
examples.solution:
The number of packs must divide both 27 and 45 exactly.

Write \(27=3^{3}\) and \(45=3^{2}\times 5\). Keep only the shared copies of primes.

The HCF is 9. Each pack uses 3 brass and 5 steel clips.

examples.title: Find the next shared finish
examples.question: Two machines finish jobs together. One finishes every 9 seconds and the other every 12 seconds. After how many seconds do they next finish together?
examples.solution:
The first machine finishes after 9, 18, 27, and so on.

The other finishes after 12, 24, 36, and so on.

The first positive time in both lists is 36 seconds.

examples.title: Choose the correct prime copies
examples.question: Find the lowest common multiple of 24 and 40.
examples.solution:
The two prime products are \(24=2^{3}\times 3\) and \(40=2^{3}\times 5\).

Keep the greater count of every prime that appears.

Multiplying the selected copies gives \(2^{3}\times 3\times 5=120\).

lessons.title: Squares, cubes and reciprocals
lessons.summary: Recognise squares and cubes, then use multiplication to check a reciprocal.
lessons.objective: Recognise squares and cubes, then use multiplication to check a reciprocal.
lessons.before: Read one worked example. Cover the next step, try it, then compare your method.
lessons.ideas:
The square-root symbol gives the non-negative root.

Cubing a negative number gives a negative cube. Its real cube root is negative.

To find the reciprocal of a non-zero fraction, interchange the numerator and denominator.
lessons.method:
Why is a square number called a square?

A square grid has the same number of rows and columns. The total number of tiles is the square of the side length. The square root returns the side length.

What does a third factor do?

A cube has the same number of rows, columns and layers. The cube of any number multiplies three copies. The cube root undoes this.

Which number will multiply to make one?

A reciprocal undoes multiplication. Multiply the starting number by its reciprocal and the result is 1.
mistakes: A power of 2 tells you to multiply the number by itself. For example, doubling 5 gives 10, while squaring it gives 25.
A negative value has a real cube root. It has no real square root.
Zero has no reciprocal because multiplying by zero always gives zero.

examples.title: Read a square root
examples.question: Evaluate \(\sqrt{16}\).
examples.solution:
Look for an equal-side square with 16 tiles.

\(4\times4=16\) gives the side length.

The symbol asks for the non-negative root, so use 4.

examples.title: Undo a negative cube
examples.question: Evaluate \(\sqrt[3]{-27}\).
examples.solution:
Three negative factors multiply to a negative number.

\((-3)^3=-27\) gives the required cube.

The cube root is \(-3\).

examples.title: Find the reciprocal
examples.question: Find the exact reciprocal of \(\frac{9}{13}\).
examples.solution:
The reciprocal is the factor that makes the product equal to 1.

Swap the numerator and denominator to get \(\frac{13}{9}\).

Check \(\frac{9}{13}\times \frac{13}{9}=1\).

1. Let \(N=2^{4}\times 3^{2}\times 5\times 7^{3}\). Find the smallest positive integer that makes a square when multiplied by \(N\).

    Show the method you used.

    [2]

  2. Write 552 as a product of prime factors in index form.

    Show the method you used.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

A square repeats the same list of factors twice. Every prime exponent must be even.

These primes have odd exponents: 5, 7. Each needs one more copy.

Multiply the needed primes. The smallest multiplier is 35.

(b)

Split off 2 while the remaining number is even.

The prime factors in order are \(2\times 2\times 2\times 3\times 23\).

The compact form is \(552=2^{3}\times 3\times 23\). The exponent on 2 is 3.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Find the primes with odd exponents and give each one more copy.

(b)

Count the prime 2 each time it appears at the end of a branch.

1. Evaluate \(\sqrt{1521}\).

    Show the method you used.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact reciprocal of \(\frac{81}{121}\).

    Show the method you used.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Look for an equal-side square with 1521 tiles.

\(39\times39=1521\) gives the side length.

The symbol asks for the non-negative root, so use 39.

(b)

The reciprocal is the factor that makes the product equal to 1.

Swap the numerator and denominator to get \(\frac{121}{81}\).

Check \(\frac{81}{121}\times \frac{121}{81}=1\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Find the number that makes the stated square.

(b)

Swap the top and bottom, then check the product.

marking_criteria.description_html: Swap the numerator and denominator to get \(\frac{121}{81}\).

    Show the method you used.

    [2]

  2. Evaluate \(\sqrt[3]{-79507}\).

    Show the method you used.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The reciprocal is the factor that makes the product equal to 1.

Swap the numerator and denominator to get \(\frac{121}{81}\).

Check \(\frac{81}{121}\times \frac{121}{81}=1\).

(b)

Three negative factors multiply to a negative number.

\((-43)^3=-79507\) gives the required cube.

The cube root is \(-43\).

(b)
